2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	The experiments in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}--\ref{sec:consensus_validation} reveal that lead-lag conclusions in iterative training collapse are fragile along multiple axes.
5	This section distills three methodological pitfalls (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}), proposes a multi-method consensus framework to address them (\S\ref{sec:consensus}), and calibrates the framework's error rates using built-in experimental controls (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
6	
7	
8	\subsection{Methodological Pitfalls in Lead-Lag Analysis}
9	\label{sec:pitfalls}
10	
11	We identify three pitfalls that, individually or in combination, can produce incorrect conclusions about temporal precedence in iterative training systems.
12	Each is documented below with representative data from our experiments; full results appear in \S\ref{sec:experiments}.
13	
14	\paragraph{Pitfall 1: Method sensitivity.}
15	Applied to the same data ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs---4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics, including candidates later excluded per \S\ref{sec:case_study}), five lead-lag detection methods yield FDR significance rates ranging from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 25\% (Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality), with inter-method agreement of Cohen's $\kappa{=}0.185$---poor agreement (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
16	The spurious-signal rate---the fraction of pairs flagged by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative---is 75\% across all five methods and 62.5\% when excluding Toda--Yamamoto, whose low statistical power at $T{=}10$ inflates this rate.
17	This pitfall is dangerous because method choice alone can determine whether a lead-lag relationship is deemed present or absent.
18	In a literature where single-method analyses are the norm, the implicit assumption that method choice does not matter is demonstrably false.
19	
20	\paragraph{Pitfall 2: Spurious regression under shared trends.}
21	A single preprocessing decision---first-differencing to remove shared non-stationary trends~\cite{granger1974spurious}---can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
22	At $\alpha{=}1.0$, canary$\to$perplexity pairs appear near-universally significant in undifferenced analysis ($F{=}16$--$36$) but yield $F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a; \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
23	In contrast, canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24).
24	Without the differencing diagnostic, an analyst would conclude that canaries predict perplexity---a conclusion entirely driven by co-trending rather than temporal precedence.
25	The danger lies in the selective nature of this confound: only by applying the diagnostic can one determine which channels are genuine and which are artifacts of shared non-stationarity.
26	
27	\paragraph{Pitfall 3: Regime dependence.}
28	Even after fixing the statistical method, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a lead-lag relationship is detectable.
29	Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH FDR-corrected at $q{=}0.05$) find 6/8 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha{=}1.0$ but 0/8 at all $\alpha{\leq}0.50$ (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
30	The $\alpha{=}0.50$ regime is particularly dangerous: correlation-based methods unanimously find significance while causal methods unanimously find non-significance (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}), creating the maximum risk of spurious conclusions---high correlation coexists with zero causal precedence.
31	This regime dependence is consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short ecological time series \cite{boettiger2012limits}, and suggests that detectability boundaries should be explicitly mapped rather than assumed.
32	
33	
34	\subsection{Multi-Method Consensus Framework}
35	\label{sec:consensus}
36	
37	The pitfalls above motivate a consensus approach inspired by multi-method validation practices in early-warning signal detection \cite{scheffer2009early}: rather than relying on any single method, we require agreement across multiple independent methods and random seeds before classifying a lead-lag relationship as robust.
38	
39	\paragraph{Formal definition.}
40	Given $M$ lead-lag detection methods $\{m_1, \ldots, m_M\}$ and $N$ independent random seeds, a canary$\to$downstream pair $(X, Y)$ is classified as \textsc{robust} if and only if:
41	\begin{enumerate}
42	    \item At least $K$ of $M$ methods judge the pair FDR-significant, where each method independently applies Benjamini--Hochberg correction at $q{=}0.05$; and
43	    \item At least $S$ of $N$ seeds replicate this conclusion.
44	\end{enumerate}
45	The thresholds $(K, S)$ control the trade-off between false positive and false negative rates.
46	Methods with different inductive biases---correlation-based methods that detect any temporal association versus Granger-type methods that test directional predictive improvement \cite{granger1969investigating}---provide complementary evidence.
47	Their convergence on a given pair constitutes stronger evidence than agreement among methods sharing the same statistical assumptions.
48	We note that Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality \cite{shojaie2022granger}; our framework inherits this limitation.
49	
50	\paragraph{Sequential filtering pipeline.}
51	We instantiate the framework as a four-stage pipeline (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}):
52	\begin{enumerate}
53	    \item \textbf{Naive correlation scan.} Cross-correlation at maximum lag~5 with BH correction serves as a permissive baseline; all pairs with any temporal association pass.

55	    \item \textbf{Permutation Granger causality.} Permutation-based Granger causality tests \cite{shojaie2022granger} on first-differenced series (5{,}000 permutations, BH correction at $q{=}0.05$) assess directional predictive improvement: whether past values of $X$ improve prediction of $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history.
56	    \item \textbf{Multi-seed replication.} The conclusion must hold across $S$ of $N$ independent training seeds, filtering seed-specific artifacts.
57	\end{enumerate}
58	At $\alpha{=}1.0$, this pipeline progressively filters: 16 pairs pass Stage~1, 14 survive Stage~2 (differencing removes 2 marginal canary$\to$perplexity pairs), 6 survive Stage~3 (Granger testing eliminates remaining canary$\to$perplexity pairs and failed canary candidates), and all~6 survive Stage~4 (multi-seed replication confirms all Granger-significant pairs).

102	    \item[(a)] The canary$\to$downstream drift ratio at $\alpha{=}1.0$ must exceed $3\times$ the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline drift (canary ratios: entropy $11.93\times$, ECE $73.12\times$---both far above threshold); and

This section distills three methodological pitfalls (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}), proposes a multi-method consensus framework to address them (\S\ref{sec:consensus}), and calibrates the framework's error rates using built-in experimental controls (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).


\subsection{Methodological Pitfalls in Lead-Lag Analysis}
\label{sec:pitfalls}

We identify three pitfalls that, individually or in combination, can produce incorrect conclusions about temporal precedence in iterative training systems.
Each is documented below with representative data from our experiments; full results appear in \S\ref{sec:experiments}.

\paragraph{Pitfall 1: Method sensitivity.}
Applied to the same data ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs---4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics, including candidates later excluded per \S\ref{sec:case_study}), five lead-lag detection methods yield FDR significance rates ranging from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 25\% (Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality), with inter-method agreement of Cohen's $\kappa{=}0.185$---poor agreement (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
The spurious-signal rate---the fraction of pairs flagged by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative---is 75\% across all five methods and 62.5\% when excluding Toda--Yamamoto, whose low statistical power at $T{=}10$ inflates this rate.
This pitfall is dangerous because method choice alone can determine whether a lead-lag relationship is deemed present or absent.
In a literature where single-method analyses are the norm, the implicit assumption that method choice does not matter is demonstrably false.

\paragraph{Pitfall 2: Spurious regression under shared trends.}
A single preprocessing decision---first-differencing to remove shared non-stationary trends~\cite{granger1974spurious}---can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, canary$\to$perplexity pairs appear near-universally significant in undifferenced analysis ($F{=}16$--$36$) but yield $F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a; \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
In contrast, canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24).
Without the differencing diagnostic, an analyst would conclude that canaries predict perplexity---a conclusion entirely driven by co-trending rather than temporal precedence.
The danger lies in the selective nature of this confound: only by applying the diagnostic can one determine which channels are genuine and which are artifacts of shared non-stationarity.

\paragraph{Pitfall 3: Regime dependence.}
Even after fixing the statistical method, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a lead-lag relationship is detectable.
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH FDR-corrected at $q{=}0.05$) find 6/8 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha{=}1.0$ but 0/8 at all $\alpha{\leq}0.50$ (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
The $\alpha{=}0.50$ regime is particularly dangerous: correlation-based methods unanimously find significance while causal methods unanimously find non-significance (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}), creating the maximum risk of spurious conclusions---high correlation coexists with zero causal precedence.
This regime dependence is consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short ecological time series \cite{boettiger2012limits}, and suggests that detectability boundaries should be explicitly mapped rather than assumed.


\subsection{Multi-Method Consensus Framework}
\label{sec:consensus}

The pitfalls above motivate a consensus approach inspired by multi-method validation practices in early-warning signal detection \cite{scheffer2009early}: rather than relying on any single method, we require agreement across multiple independent methods and random seeds before classifying a lead-lag relationship as robust.

\paragraph{Formal definition.}
Given $M$ lead-lag detection methods $\{m_1, \ldots, m_M\}$ and $N$ independent random seeds, a canary$\to$downstream pair $(X, Y)$ is classified as \textsc{robust} if and only if:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item At least $K$ of $M$ methods judge the pair FDR-significant, where each method independently applies Benjamini--Hochberg correction at $q{=}0.05$; and
    \item At least $S$ of $N$ seeds replicate this conclusion.
\end{enumerate}
The thresholds $(K, S)$ control the trade-off between false positive and false negative rates.
Methods with different inductive biases---correlation-based methods that detect any temporal association versus Granger-type methods that test directional predictive improvement \cite{granger1969investigating}---provide complementary evidence.
Their convergence on a given pair constitutes stronger evidence than agreement among methods sharing the same statistical assumptions.
We note that Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality \cite{shojaie2022granger}; our framework inherits this limitation.

\paragraph{Sequential filtering pipeline.}
We instantiate the framework as a four-stage pipeline (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}):
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Naive correlation scan.} Cross-correlation at maximum lag~5 with BH correction serves as a permissive baseline; all pairs with any temporal association pass.
    \item \textbf{First-differencing diagnostic.} Cross-correlation is recomputed on first-differenced series, testing whether temporal associations survive removal of shared linear trends. Pairs that lose significance are flagged as potential spurious regressions.
    \item \textbf{Permutation Granger causality.} Permutation-based Granger causality tests \cite{shojaie2022granger} on first-differenced series (5{,}000 permutations, BH correction at $q{=}0.05$) assess directional predictive improvement: whether past values of $X$ improve prediction of $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history.
    \item \textbf{Multi-seed replication.} The conclusion must hold across $S$ of $N$ independent training seeds, filtering seed-specific artifacts.
\end{enumerate}
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, this pipeline progressively filters: 16 pairs pass Stage~1, 14 survive Stage~2 (differencing removes 2 marginal canary$\to$perplexity pairs), 6 survive Stage~3 (Granger testing eliminates remaining canary$\to$perplexity pairs and failed canary candidates), and all~6 survive Stage~4 (multi-seed replication confirms all Granger-significant pairs).

\paragraph{Practical guidance.}
The consensus thresholds $(K, S)$ should be chosen to match the analyst's tolerance for false positives versus false negatives.
Table~\ref{tab:practical_guidance} provides four recommended tiers, calibrated against our experimental controls (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
Tier~3 ($K{\geq}4/5$, $S{\geq}3/4$) achieves the best trade-off in our setting: zero false positives while recovering all six reference pairs.
Method subset ablation confirms that this threshold is uniquely optimal: at $K{=}3/5$, the null-control FPR is 50\% (unacceptable); at $K{=}4/5$, FPR drops to 0\% while retaining 6/6 reference-pair sensitivity; at $K{=}5/5$, FPR remains 0\% but sensitivity falls to 3/6.
Shapley value analysis identifies permutation Granger causality as the linchpin method (Shapley $= +0.375$), the only method combining 0\% null-control FPR with high sensitivity.
Toda--Yamamoto contributes negatively (Shapley $= -2.625$) due to its Type~II errors at $T{=}10$; we retain it as insurance against unknown integration order in our consensus panel, but note its severe power limitations at $T{\leq}10$ and caution that its results should be interpreted accordingly.
Tier~4 requires unanimity across methods and seeds, which incurs a 50\% false negative rate because Toda--Yamamoto produces Type~II errors at $T{=}10$ due to insufficient residual degrees of freedom (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).

\centering
\small
\caption{Practical guidance tiers for lead-lag consensus analysis. FPR is calibrated at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (null control, $M{=}5$ methods). FNR is calibrated at $\alpha{=}1.0$ against 6 effect-size reference pairs using a 4-method panel (excluding differenced cross-correlation); $N{=}4$ seeds (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).}
\label{tab:practical_guidance}
\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
\toprule
Tier & Use Case & $K/M$ & $S/N$ & FPR & FNR \\
\midrule
1 & Exploratory     & ${\geq}1/5$ & ${\geq}1/N$ & 100\%  & 0\%    \\
2 & Screening       & ${\geq}3/5$ & ${\geq}2/N$ & 37.5\% & 0\%    \\
3 & Confirmatory    & ${\geq}4/5$ & ${\geq}3/N$ & 0\%    & 0\%    \\
4 & Conservative    & $5/5$       & $N/N$        & 0\%    & 50\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


\subsection{Empirical Calibration}
\label{sec:calibration}

We calibrate the framework using two built-in experimental controls.
Full numerical results are reported in Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr}.

\paragraph{False positive rate.}
The $\alpha{=}0.0$ condition serves as a null control: no synthetic data is injected, so any detected lead-lag association is a false positive.
At $K{=}1$ (any single method suffices), FPR${=}$100\%---naive cross-correlation alone flags all pairs.
At $K{=}2$, FPR drops to 75\%; at $K{=}3$, to 37.5\%; and at $K{\geq}4$, FPR${=}$0\%.
The consensus framework at Tier~3 matches the false positive performance of the best individual methods (permutation Granger and Toda--Yamamoto, both 0\%) while providing robustness against miscalibration of any single method.

\paragraph{False negative rate.}
At $\alpha{=}1.0$ with 4~seeds, we define six \emph{effect-size reference pairs} using criteria independent of the consensus methods:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] The canary$\to$downstream drift ratio at $\alpha{=}1.0$ must exceed $3\times$ the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline drift (canary ratios: entropy $11.93\times$, ECE $73.12\times$---both far above threshold); and
    \item[(b)] Canary onset must strictly precede downstream onset by at least one generation (canary onset: generation~1; diversity onset: generations~3--9).
\end{enumerate}
These criteria yield token entropy and ECE each predicting distinct-1, distinct-2, and distinct-3~\cite{li2016diversity}.
The perplexity channel is excluded because its onset (generation~1) coincides with canary onset, consistent with---but not derived from---the differencing diagnostic finding that canary$\to$perplexity associations are spurious (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
The effect-size threshold is robust: at $2\times$, $3\times$, and $5\times$ the baseline drift, the reference set remains identical (6~pairs), because canary ratios ($11.93\times$ and $73.12\times$) far exceed all thresholds.

FNR is calibrated using a 4-method panel excluding differenced cross-correlation, which shares statistical properties with detrending-based criteria and could introduce circularity.
At $K{\geq}3/4$, $S{\geq}3/4$, all six reference pairs are recovered (FNR${=}$0\%).
At $K{=}4/4$, $S{=}4/4$, FNR rises to 50\% because Toda--Yamamoto produces Type~II errors at $T{=}10$ due to insufficient residual degrees of freedom (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).

\paragraph{Design asymmetry.}
FPR is validated on the method dimension only (single seed at $\alpha{=}0.0$), while FNR is validated on the joint method${\times}$seed dimension (4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
Full joint calibration---multi-seed null-control experiments---remains future work.
This asymmetry means that FPR estimates may be optimistic if seed-level variance in false positive rates is non-negligible.

4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
8	Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across five contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
9	Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
10	Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.
11	
12	Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
13	Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
14	We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
15	The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha{=}0.25$ uses three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; other conditions use seed~42.
16	
17	We track two \emph{canary metrics}---cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}---and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
18	Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
19	Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).

22	Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
23	Code and data will be released upon publication.
24	
25	All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.

49	\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
50	\label{sec:method_sensitivity}
51	
52	We open with Claim~3---method sensitivity---because it conditions the interpretation of all subsequent results.

107	\subsection{Regime-Dependent Detectability}
108	\label{sec:regime}
109	
110	Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.
111	We present regime effects at two levels: raw metric drift (method-independent) and Granger-precedence detectability.
112	
113	\paragraph{Raw drift.}
114	Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} shows that diversity collapse occurs at \emph{all} contamination levels, not only under full synthetic replacement.
115	Distinct-1 declines by 13.8\% even at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (attributable to fine-tuning on repeated real-data subsets), and more steeply at intermediate contamination: $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.25$), $-37.3\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $-32.7\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.75$), and $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$ ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
116	The non-monotonic pattern---diversity declining \emph{more} at moderate~$\alpha$ than at extreme~$\alpha$---is confirmed by 3-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (std${=}0.3\%$), indicating that this relationship between contamination level and collapse severity is robust rather than a seed-specific artifact.
117	
118	\paragraph{Granger-precedence detectability.}
119	Despite ubiquitous drift, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
120	Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH-corrected) find 0/8 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha{=}0.00$, 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.25$, 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, and \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}1.0$ in the cross-$\alpha$ pooled analysis.
121	At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (single seed, seed=42), 3/8 pairs reach FDR significance; this result requires multi-seed replication before serving as primary evidence.
122	Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.
123	The detectability boundary---the regime below which canary metrics no longer develop sufficient temporal lead for causal inference---lies at $\alpha \approx 0.50$--$0.75$, consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short time series \cite{boettiger2012limits}.
124	This boundary is sharp rather than gradual: method-level consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) identifies 0--1 of 16 candidate pairs as robust at $\alpha{\leq}0.50$ but 11/16 at $\alpha{=}0.75$ (single seed, pre-pipeline filtering; the stricter $K{\geq}4/5$, $S{\geq}3/4$ criterion at $\alpha{=}1.0$ retains 6/16 after excluding failed candidates and spurious channels per \S\ref{sec:case_study}).

128	\paragraph{Synchronous collapse at $\alpha{=}0.50$.}

130	Correlation-based methods unanimously find significance (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}) while causal methods unanimously find non-significance.

136	\subsection{Case Study: Canary Prediction of Diversity Collapse}
137	\label{sec:case_study}
138	
139	Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
140	We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.
141	
142	\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
143	Token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse metrics, confirmed by 4 independent statistical methods (permutation Granger power${=}1.0$), 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium (Tier~3 consensus; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
144	Cross-correlation peaks at lag$={+}1$ with $|r|{>}0.99$ (cross-seed standard deviation: 0.0), establishing a consistent one-generation lead.
145	Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory} illustrates the one-generation offset between token entropy decline and distinct-1 decline, visible across all four seeds.
146	Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced) confirm all canary$\to$diversity pairs as FDR-significant across all four seeds, including distinct-3 (Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}).
147	Reverse-direction tests (downstream$\to$canary) find \textbf{0/24} FDR-significant (all $p{>}0.49$), establishing complete directional asymmetry.
148	
149	\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, single seed).}
150	At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (seed=42), three of four forward-direction pairs reach FDR significance: ECE$\to$distinct-1 ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.046$), ECE$\to$distinct-2 ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.046$), and token entropy$\to$distinct-2 ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.048$).
151	Token entropy$\to$distinct-1 is borderline ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.054$).
152	All four reverse directions are non-significant ($p{>}0.49$).
153	These single-seed results require multi-seed confirmation before serving as primary evidence.
154	
155	\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
156	ECE performs equivalently to token entropy across four of five methods (naive, differenced, threshold, permutation Granger).
157	Its classification as ``secondary'' is driven entirely by Toda--Yamamoto Type~II errors at $T{=}10$, where bootstrap power analysis yields estimated power of 0.05--0.20 depending on $d_{\max}$.
158	Resolving ECE's true canary status requires longer time series.
159	
160	\paragraph{Failed canary candidates.}
161	Not all metrics serve as canaries.
162	Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.
163	Whether their failure as canaries is model-dependent---effective rank in particular reflects representational geometry that may vary across architectures---remains an open question.
164	
165	\paragraph{Consensus filtering.}
166	Of 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs tested at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics), \textbf{6 survive} the full consensus pipeline ($K{\geq}4/5$ methods, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds): token entropy and ECE each predicting distinct-1 and distinct-2 (4 pairs; distinct-3 results in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3} bring the total to~6).
167	The 10 eliminated pairs comprise all canary$\to$perplexity relationships (identified as spurious by the first-differencing diagnostic) and all effective-rank and Self-BLEU pairs (failed canaries).
168	The consensus framework reduces the naive 100\% significance rate to the 37.5\% rate supported by the most conservative individual methods (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}).

171	\subsection{Consensus Framework Validation}
172	\label{sec:consensus_validation}
173	
174	We validate the consensus framework's calibration using built-in experimental controls.
175	
176	\paragraph{False positive rate.}
177	At $\alpha{=}0.0$, no synthetic data is injected; any detected lead-lag association is a false positive.
178	Individual-method FPR ranges from \textbf{100\%} (naive cross-correlation: 8/8 pairs) through 62.5\% (threshold) and 37.5\% (differenced) down to \textbf{0\%} (permutation Granger and Toda--Yamamoto).
179	The consensus framework at $K{\geq}4/5$ achieves \textbf{FPR${=}$0\%}, matching the best individual methods while providing robustness against miscalibration of any single method (Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr}).
180	
181	\paragraph{False negative rate.}
182	At $\alpha{=}1.0$, we define 6 effect-size reference pairs (token entropy and ECE $\to$ distinct-1/2/3) using criteria independent of the consensus methods: drift ratio ${\geq}3\times$ the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline (entropy $11.93\times$, ECE $73.12\times$) and canary onset strictly preceding downstream onset by ${\geq}1$ generation (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
183	FNR is calibrated on a 4-method panel (excluding differenced cross-correlation to avoid circularity): at $K{\geq}3/4$, $S{\geq}3/4$, all~6 are recovered (\textbf{FNR${=}$0\%}).
184	Toda--Yamamoto alone yields FNR${=}$33.3\% (2/6), missing ECE$\to$distinct-2 and ECE$\to$distinct-3 due to Type~II errors at $T{=}10$.
185	We note a design asymmetry: FPR is validated on method-only data (single seed at $\alpha{=}0.0$), while FNR uses method$\times$seed joint data (4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
186	Full joint calibration---multi-seed null-control experiments---remains future work.
187	Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr} reports the calibration results.
188	
189	\paragraph{Bootstrap power analysis.}
190	To quantify detection power beyond binary FNR, we perform bootstrap power analysis ($B{=}1{,}000$ resamples from 4-seed data at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
191	Permutation Granger achieves power${=}1.0$ on genuine pairs (canary$\to$diversity) and power${=}0.0$ on spurious pairs (canary$\to$perplexity), providing clean separation.
192	Toda--Yamamoto achieves power${=}0.05$--$0.20$ on genuine pairs (depending on $d_{\max}$), confirming its poor sensitivity at $T{=}10$.
193	We note that bootstrap power${=}1.0$ reflects the effect size in our 4-seed data and should not be interpreted as a universal power guarantee; furthermore, the two methods use different data-generating processes for calibration (permutation Granger resamples observed $\alpha{=}1.0$ trajectories, while Toda--Yamamoto power was estimated under a generic VAR(2) simulation with $\beta{=}0.3$).

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across five contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.

Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.

Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
Code and data will be released upon publication.

All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.

Restricting to three informative methods (excluding naive cross-correlation and Toda--Yamamoto, which anchor the permissive and conservative extremes respectively) raises $\kappa$ to 0.667 (substantial agreement), indicating that the low full-panel $\kappa$ is driven by the deliberate inclusion of methods spanning the entire permissive-to-conservative spectrum rather than by fundamental incoherence among methods.
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} extends the analysis across contamination levels.
At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (no synthetic data, serving as null control), naive cross-correlation finds \textbf{100\%} of pairs significant---a textbook spurious-regression outcome in trending time series.
Permutation Granger and Toda--Yamamoto correctly find 0\%.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$, correlation-based methods (naive, differenced, threshold) unanimously find significance while causal methods unanimously find non-significance (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}), the most extreme method$\times$regime divergence in our experiments.

\paragraph{Method$\times$regime interaction.}
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reveals that the correlation-versus-causal divergence is not uniform across contamination levels.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, differenced cross-correlation drops to 25\% and threshold onset to 37.5\%, while naive cross-correlation remains at 100\%---demonstrating that even partial detrending removes marginal associations at low contamination.
In low-contamination regimes ($\alpha{\leq}0.50$), the false confirmation rate for the most liberal method approaches 100\%, while all Granger-type tests correctly find 0\%---a regime where single-method analysis is maximally dangerous.

\subsection{Regime-Dependent Detectability}
\label{sec:regime}

Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.
We present regime effects at two levels: raw metric drift (method-independent) and Granger-precedence detectability.

\paragraph{Raw drift.}
Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} shows that diversity collapse occurs at \emph{all} contamination levels, not only under full synthetic replacement.
Distinct-1 declines by 13.8\% even at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (attributable to fine-tuning on repeated real-data subsets), and more steeply at intermediate contamination: $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.25$), $-37.3\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $-32.7\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.75$), and $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$ ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
The non-monotonic pattern---diversity declining \emph{more} at moderate~$\alpha$ than at extreme~$\alpha$---is confirmed by 3-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (std${=}0.3\%$), indicating that this relationship between contamination level and collapse severity is robust rather than a seed-specific artifact.

\paragraph{Granger-precedence detectability.}
Despite ubiquitous drift, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH-corrected) find 0/8 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha{=}0.00$, 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.25$, 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, and \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}1.0$ in the cross-$\alpha$ pooled analysis.
At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (single seed, seed=42), 3/8 pairs reach FDR significance; this result requires multi-seed replication before serving as primary evidence.
Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.
The detectability boundary---the regime below which canary metrics no longer develop sufficient temporal lead for causal inference---lies at $\alpha \approx 0.50$--$0.75$, consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short time series \cite{boettiger2012limits}.
This boundary is sharp rather than gradual: method-level consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) identifies 0--1 of 16 candidate pairs as robust at $\alpha{\leq}0.50$ but 11/16 at $\alpha{=}0.75$ (single seed, pre-pipeline filtering; the stricter $K{\geq}4/5$, $S{\geq}3/4$ criterion at $\alpha{=}1.0$ retains 6/16 after excluding failed candidates and spurious channels per \S\ref{sec:case_study}).
The lower count at $\alpha{=}1.0$ despite stronger contamination reflects the stricter validation standard: multi-seed replication ($S{\geq}3/4$) filters seed-specific artifacts, and pipeline filtering removes the perplexity channel (spurious per \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}) and failed canary candidates (effective rank, Self-BLEU), both of which contribute to the $\alpha{=}0.75$ single-seed count.
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium confirms this boundary: at $\alpha{=}0.25$, 0/8 pairs reach Confirmatory consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) despite substantially stronger canary drift (entropy $-32.8\%$ vs.\ Pythia $-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$), while at $\alpha{=}1.0$ all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach $K{\geq}4/5$ (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Synchronous collapse at $\alpha{=}0.50$.}
The $\alpha{=}0.50$ regime provides particularly informative evidence.
Correlation-based methods unanimously find significance (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}) while causal methods unanimously find non-significance.
This extreme method$\times$regime interaction arises because canary and downstream metrics collapse \emph{synchronously} at moderate contamination, preserving high correlation but eliminating the temporal lead required for Granger-precedence inference.
We highlight this as a \emph{positive finding}: it delineates the regime boundary where naive analysis is most dangerous---high correlation coexists with zero causal precedence, maximizing the risk of spurious conclusions.
Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap} visualizes this interaction across all method$\times\alpha$ combinations, revealing a clear block structure that separates correlation-based methods from causal methods as a function of regime.


\subsection{Case Study: Canary Prediction of Diversity Collapse}
\label{sec:case_study}

Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.

\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
Token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse metrics, confirmed by 4 independent statistical methods (permutation Granger power${=}1.0$), 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium (Tier~3 consensus; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Cross-correlation peaks at lag$={+}1$ with $|r|{>}0.99$ (cross-seed standard deviation: 0.0), establishing a consistent one-generation lead.
Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory} illustrates the one-generation offset between token entropy decline and distinct-1 decline, visible across all four seeds.
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced) confirm all canary$\to$diversity pairs as FDR-significant across all four seeds, including distinct-3 (Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}).
Reverse-direction tests (downstream$\to$canary) find \textbf{0/24} FDR-significant (all $p{>}0.49$), establishing complete directional asymmetry.

\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, single seed).}
At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (seed=42), three of four forward-direction pairs reach FDR significance: ECE$\to$distinct-1 ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.046$), ECE$\to$distinct-2 ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.046$), and token entropy$\to$distinct-2 ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.048$).
Token entropy$\to$distinct-1 is borderline ($p_\text{fdr}{=}0.054$).
All four reverse directions are non-significant ($p{>}0.49$).
These single-seed results require multi-seed confirmation before serving as primary evidence.

\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
ECE performs equivalently to token entropy across four of five methods (naive, differenced, threshold, permutation Granger).
Its classification as ``secondary'' is driven entirely by Toda--Yamamoto Type~II errors at $T{=}10$, where bootstrap power analysis yields estimated power of 0.05--0.20 depending on $d_{\max}$.
Resolving ECE's true canary status requires longer time series.

\paragraph{Failed canary candidates.}
Not all metrics serve as canaries.
Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.
Whether their failure as canaries is model-dependent---effective rank in particular reflects representational geometry that may vary across architectures---remains an open question.

\paragraph{Consensus filtering.}
Of 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs tested at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics), \textbf{6 survive} the full consensus pipeline ($K{\geq}4/5$ methods, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds): token entropy and ECE each predicting distinct-1 and distinct-2 (4 pairs; distinct-3 results in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3} bring the total to~6).
The 10 eliminated pairs comprise all canary$\to$perplexity relationships (identified as spurious by the first-differencing diagnostic) and all effective-rank and Self-BLEU pairs (failed canaries).
The consensus framework reduces the naive 100\% significance rate to the 37.5\% rate supported by the most conservative individual methods (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}).


\subsection{Consensus Framework Validation}
\label{sec:consensus_validation}

We validate the consensus framework's calibration using built-in experimental controls.

\paragraph{False positive rate.}
At $\alpha{=}0.0$, no synthetic data is injected; any detected lead-lag association is a false positive.
Individual-method FPR ranges from \textbf{100\%} (naive cross-correlation: 8/8 pairs) through 62.5\% (threshold) and 37.5\% (differenced) down to \textbf{0\%} (permutation Granger and Toda--Yamamoto).
The consensus framework at $K{\geq}4/5$ achieves \textbf{FPR${=}$0\%}, matching the best individual methods while providing robustness against miscalibration of any single method (Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr}).

\paragraph{False negative rate.}
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, we define 6 effect-size reference pairs (token entropy and ECE $\to$ distinct-1/2/3) using criteria independent of the consensus methods: drift ratio ${\geq}3\times$ the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline (entropy $11.93\times$, ECE $73.12\times$) and canary onset strictly preceding downstream onset by ${\geq}1$ generation (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
FNR is calibrated on a 4-method panel (excluding differenced cross-correlation to avoid circularity): at $K{\geq}3/4$, $S{\geq}3/4$, all~6 are recovered (\textbf{FNR${=}$0\%}).
Toda--Yamamoto alone yields FNR${=}$33.3\% (2/6), missing ECE$\to$distinct-2 and ECE$\to$distinct-3 due to Type~II errors at $T{=}10$.
We note a design asymmetry: FPR is validated on method-only data (single seed at $\alpha{=}0.0$), while FNR uses method$\times$seed joint data (4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
Full joint calibration---multi-seed null-control experiments---remains future work.
Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr} reports the calibration results.

\paragraph{Bootstrap power analysis.}
To quantify detection power beyond binary FNR, we perform bootstrap power analysis ($B{=}1{,}000$ resamples from 4-seed data at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
Permutation Granger achieves power${=}1.0$ on genuine pairs (canary$\to$diversity) and power${=}0.0$ on spurious pairs (canary$\to$perplexity), providing clean separation.
Toda--Yamamoto achieves power${=}0.05$--$0.20$ on genuine pairs (depending on $d_{\max}$), confirming its poor sensitivity at $T{=}10$.
We note that bootstrap power${=}1.0$ reflects the effect size in our 4-seed data and should not be interpreted as a universal power guarantee; furthermore, the two methods use different data-generating processes for calibration (permutation Granger resamples observed $\alpha{=}1.0$ trajectories, while Toda--Yamamoto power was estimated under a generic VAR(2) simulation with $\beta{=}0.3$).

Full joint calibration---requiring multi-seed null-control experiments at $\alpha{=}0.0$---remains an open direction for future work.

\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure's elevated FNR (33.3\%, missing 2 of 6 directional pairs) is attributable to insufficient residual degrees of freedom at this series length, not to a fundamental deficiency in the method itself.
This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$.
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure produces valid test statistics at all window lengths ($T \in \{5, \ldots, 10\}$), but with unstable sensitivity---3/6 to 6/6 pairs reach significance depending on window length---confirming that its elevated FNR reflects limited residual degrees of freedom rather than absence of signal.

\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method consensus: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.

\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse---but at these contamination levels, degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
At $\alpha{\leq}0.50$, where early warning would be most valuable, the canary signal is undetectable by any method tested.
This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards---tracking cumulative trend shifts across many generations---than to single-point threshold alarms.
If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.

\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data}---measuring the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text---while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text}---measuring the model's self-consistency on its own outputs.
The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}---both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.

\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods and explains the Toda--Yamamoto procedure's poor power in our setting.
Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to---rather than replacement for---traditional significance testing.

\paragraph{Future work.}
Several directions extend this work.
Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
Cross-architecture validation beyond our preliminary single-seed GPT-2-medium result requires multi-seed replication; evaluation on larger-scale models would further test generalizability.
Online monitoring---integrating canary metrics into training pipelines for real-time collapse detection---is a natural applied extension.
Accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking} would test whether canary dynamics differ from the replace-mode setting studied here.
Finally, connecting the empirically observed detectability boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.50$--$0.75$ to theoretical phase transition analysis~\cite{truong2025entropy} could yield a principled explanation for why canary signals emerge at this contamination regime rather than at lower contamination levels.

\label{sec:conclusion}

4	Several limitations constrain the generalizability of our findings.

6	\paragraph{Model scale.}
7	Our primary experiments use Pythia-410M (410M parameters); preliminary cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters).
8	Both are decoder-only transformers of similar scale, small by contemporary standards.
9	Whether the entropy-leads-diversity pattern and the consensus framework's operating thresholds hold at billion-parameter scale remains untested.
10	The batch size difference between architectures (4 for Pythia vs.\ 32 for GPT-2-medium) means each training step exposes $8\times$ more data in the latter, potentially accelerating collapse dynamics without altering the qualitative pattern.
11	
12	\paragraph{Data domain.}
13	Training data is drawn from a single domain (a WikiText-103 subset), and domain-specific distributional properties---vocabulary richness, syntactic complexity, topical diversity---may influence the coupling between canary and downstream metrics.
14	Domains with inherently low diversity (e.g., legal text, code) could exhibit different canary dynamics.
15	
16	\paragraph{Short time series ($T{=}10$).}
17	With 11 data points per series, our statistical analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
18	This limits power for all methods and makes the Toda--Yamamoto procedure particularly unreliable (power estimated at 0.05--0.20 for our effect sizes).
19	Longer generation chains would improve statistical power but impose substantial computational cost.
20	
21	\paragraph{Bivariate Granger $\neq$ causality.}
22	Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders.
23	An unobserved process---such as a latent shift in the training data distribution---could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations.
24	Our multi-method consensus framework mitigates but does not eliminate this limitation; multivariate VAR models would be required to test for confounders directly.
25	
26	\paragraph{Regime boundary uncertainty.}
27	The detectability boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.50$--$0.75$ is characterized with limited resolution (five $\alpha$ levels).

29	The $\alpha{=}0.75$ evidence is currently single-seed and awaits multi-seed confirmation.
30

4	This section establishes the formal setup and notation used throughout the paper.
5	
6	\paragraph{Iterative training loop.}
7	Let $M_0$ denote a pretrained language model and $\mathcal{D}_\text{real}$ a fixed corpus of human-written text.
8	At each generation $t \geq 1$, the model $M_{t-1}$ generates a synthetic corpus $\mathcal{D}_\text{synth}^{(t-1)}$, and the next-generation model $M_t$ is fine-tuned on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data:
9	\begin{equation}
10	    \mathcal{D}_\text{train}^{(t)} = \alpha \cdot \mathcal{D}_\text{synth}^{(t-1)} \;+\; (1{-}\alpha) \cdot \mathcal{D}_\text{real}, \quad \alpha \in [0, 1].
11	    \label{eq:mixing}
12	\end{equation}
13	The contamination level $\alpha$ controls the fraction of machine-generated text in each training round.
14	At $\alpha{=}1.0$, this reduces to the full-replacement paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, where each generation trains exclusively on the previous generation's output.
15	Iterating this process for $T$ generations yields a trajectory $M_0 \to M_1 \to \cdots \to M_T$.
16	
17	\paragraph{Metric families.}
18	We distinguish two families of metrics evaluated at each generation~$t$.
19	\emph{Canary metrics} are cheap-to-compute statistics on the model's output distribution, hypothesized to change before downstream quality degrades---analogous to early-warning indicators studied in the context of critical transitions in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}.
20	We consider two canary metrics: \emph{token entropy}, the average next-token prediction entropy over held-out samples, and \emph{expected calibration error} (ECE), which measures the discrepancy between predicted token probabilities and empirical correctness frequencies.
21	\emph{Downstream metrics} capture generation quality directly.
22	We use \emph{distinct-$n$} ($n \in \{1, 2, 3\}$), the ratio of unique $n$-grams to total $n$-grams in generated text \cite{li2016diversity}, as a measure of lexical diversity, and \emph{perplexity} on a held-out set as a measure of language modeling quality.
23	Each metric produces a time series of $T{+}1$ observations (generations $0$ through $T$).
24	
25	\paragraph{The lead-lag testing problem.}
26	Given two such time series $X = (x_0, \ldots, x_T)$ and $Y = (y_0, \ldots, y_T)$---for instance, a canary metric and a downstream metric---the central question is whether changes in $X$ temporally precede changes in $Y$.
27	This requires more than measuring correlation: the test must establish \emph{directionality} ($X \to Y$ rather than $Y \to X$) and account for confounders such as shared non-stationary trends that can produce spurious associations.
28	The classical framework for testing temporal predictive precedence is Granger causality \cite{granger1969investigating}, which asks whether past values of $X$ improve prediction of $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history.
29	We note that Granger precedence tests predictive improvement, not true causality \cite{shojaie2022granger}; this distinction is discussed further in \S\ref{sec:method}.

4	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
5	
6	\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
7	Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
8	Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process---such as a latent distributional shift in the training data---could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
9	Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.
10	Throughout this paper, ``Granger precedence'' denotes predictive improvement in a time-series forecasting sense, not a causal mechanism.
11	This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.
12	
13	\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
14	All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and five contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
15	Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
16	The consensus framework's structure---multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication---is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds ($K{\geq}4/5$ methods, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds) are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
17	For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates at these thresholds.
18	Preliminary cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (single seed, $\alpha{=}1.0$) replicates the entropy-leads-diversity pattern at Tier~3 consensus: all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach $K{\geq}4/5$ method agreement (permutation Granger $p_{\text{FDR}}{=}0.003$), with 0/6 reverse-direction pairs significant.
19	Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
20	At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 1/8 pairs at Tier~3 consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) and 7/8 at Tier~2 ($K{\geq}3/5$), placing it in the same null/low-detectability regime as Pythia (0/8 Tier~3) and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across two transformer decoder-only model families of similar scale (\texttt{gen\_wiki\_gpt2m\_a025\_s42}).
21	The full GPT-2-medium drift profile at $\alpha{=}0.25$ is: entropy $-32.8\%$, ECE $+422\%$, perplexity $-44.5\%$, distinct-1 $-23.5\%$, distinct-2 $-31.6\%$, distinct-3 $-30.2\%$, MAUVE $0.0315 \to 0.0282$ ($-10.5\%$).
22	Compared to Pythia ($-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$ entropy, $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ distinct-1), GPT-2-medium shows substantially stronger canary drift but milder diversity decline---likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step.
23	The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.
24	Toda--Yamamoto Granger finds 1/8 pairs significant, consistent with its known instability at short series lengths (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
25	
26	\paragraph{FPR/FNR calibration asymmetry.}
27	The FPR and FNR estimates in our calibration analysis differ in their coverage of the seed dimension.
28	FPR is validated on the method dimension only, using a single seed at the null-control condition ($\alpha{=}0.0$).
29	FNR is validated on the joint method${\times}$seed dimension, aggregating across four seeds at full contamination ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
30	This asymmetry means our FPR estimate of 0\% may be optimistic: if seed-level variance in false positive rates is non-negligible, the true FPR under the consensus rule could exceed zero.
31	Full joint calibration---requiring multi-seed null-control experiments at $\alpha{=}0.0$---remains an open direction for future work.
32	
33	\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
34	With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
35	This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
36	The Toda--Yamamoto procedure's elevated FNR (33.3\%, missing 2 of 6 directional pairs) is attributable to insufficient residual degrees of freedom at this series length, not to a fundamental deficiency in the method itself.
37	This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
38	Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
39	However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:window_sensitivity}).
40	The Toda--Yamamoto procedure produces valid test statistics at all window lengths ($T \in \{5, \ldots, 10\}$), but with unstable sensitivity---3/6 to 6/6 pairs reach significance depending on window length---confirming that its elevated FNR reflects limited residual degrees of freedom rather than absence of signal.
41	
42	\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
43	Effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
44	In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
45	In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%; \texttt{gen\_wiki\_gpt2m\_a025\_s42}).
46	The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
47	This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines.
48	We note this as a caveat on the generality of representational metrics as collapse indicators, even when the regime map (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime}) and lead-lag detectability are consistent across architectures.
49	
50	\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
51	Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
52	Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).

55	\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
56	The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
57	At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse---but at these contamination levels, degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.

61	If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.

Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process---such as a latent distributional shift in the training data---could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.

This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.

All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and five contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).

The FPR and FNR estimates in our calibration analysis differ in their coverage of the seed dimension.
FPR is validated on the method dimension only, using a single seed at the null-control condition ($\alpha{=}0.0$).
FNR is validated on the joint method${\times}$seed dimension, aggregating across four seeds at full contamination ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
This asymmetry means our FPR estimate of 0\% may be optimistic: if seed-level variance in false positive rates is non-negligible, the true FPR under the consensus rule could exceed zero.
Full joint calibration---requiring multi-seed null-control experiments at $\alpha{=}0.0$---remains an open direction for future work.

\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure's elevated FNR (33.3\%, missing 2 of 6 directional pairs) is attributable to insufficient residual degrees of freedom at this series length, not to a fundamental deficiency in the method itself.

At $\alpha{\leq}0.50$, where early warning would be most valuable, the canary signal is undetectable by any method tested.

These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to---rather than replacement for---traditional significance testing.
